slides.title: What is an Interface?

blocks.text: An interface is a class-like construct that contains only
abstract methods and constants.
In many ways, an interface is like an abstract class.
The purpose of an interface is to specify common behavior for objects.
For example, you can specify that objects are comparable, edible, cloneable using appropriate interfaces.

slides.title: An Interface is a Special Abstract Class

blocks.text: An interface is treated like a special abstract class in Java.
All the methods of an interface are abstract.
You can use an interface as a data type for a variable.
Like an abstract class, you cannot create an instance of an interface using the new operator.
Each interface is compiled into a separate bytecode file, just like a regular class.

slides.title: The Comparable Interface

blocks.text: The generic Comparable interface defines the compareTo method for comparing two objects of the same type T.
The generic compareTo method can be used to compare two strings, two dates, two students, two circles, etc.
// Interface for comparing objects in java.lang
package java.lang;

public interface Comparable<T> {
  public int compareTo(T obj);

slides.title: Comparing Objects of the same Type

blocks.text: The compareTo method compares objects of the same type.
int result = object1.compareTo(object2);
The result is zero if object1 and object2 are equal The result is negative if object1 is less than object2 The result is positive if object1 is greater than object2
Examples:

slides.title: Implementing the Comparable Interface

blocks.text: Any class that implements the Comparable interface must provide an implementation of the compareTo method.

slides.title: Sorting Arrays of Objects

blocks.text: The Arrays.sort(Object[] array) method in the java.util package can sort an array of objects.
The Array.sort method uses the compareTo method to compare and sort the array elements.
Any class that implements the Comparable interface and the compareTo method can use the Array.sort method.

slides.title: Interfaces versus Abstract Classes

blocks.text: Interface Abstract Class
Can have only static final constants Can have all types of data
Can only define method signatures with no implementation
Can define methods with or without implementation
No constructors Can have constructors
An interface can extend other interfaces, but not classes
A class can extend its superclass and implement multiple interfaces
Both an interface and an abstract class cannot be instantiated using the new operator.

slides.title: Interfaces versus Abstract Classes

blocks.text: All classes share a single root, which is the Object class.
However, there is no root for interfaces.
All the data and methods of an interface are public.
However, there is no restriction for abstract classes.
If a class implements an interface, then the interface becomes like a superclass for the class.
You can use an interface as a data type and cast a variable of an interface type to its subclass, and vice versa.

slides.title: Whether to use an Interface or Class

blocks.text: Abstract classes and interfaces can both be used to specify common behavior. When to use an interface or abstract class?
In general, a strong is-a relationship should be modeled using classes. For example, a Gregorian calendar is a Calendar.
A weak is-a relationship, also known as is-kind-of relationship, can be modeled using interfaces. All strings are comparable, so the String class implements the Comparable interface.
In general, interfaces are preferred over abstract classes because an interface can define a common supertype for unrelated classes.

slides.title: Caution: Conflicting Interfaces

blocks.text: In rare occasions, a class may implement two interfaces with conflicting constant names or methods.
Two named constants are conflicting if they have the same name but different values.
Two methods are conflicting if they have the same signature but different return type.
These type of errors will be detected by the compiler.

slides.title: Case Study: The Rational Class

blocks.text: A rational number has the form a/b, where a is the numerator and b is the denominator.
Rational numbers are used to compute exact fractions.
For example, 1/3, 2/7, and 10/3 are rational numbers.
A rational number cannot have a denominator of 0.
An integer i is equivalent to a rational number i/1.
Since rational numbers are comparable, the Rational class should implement the Comparable interface.
